column3: Directly joins sacrificial livestock, Allah's name, eating, and feeding the poor in the same Hajj setting.
The rebuking formation gives only an abstract ordered-action resonance with the standing animals.
Its ordered ranks illuminate sawaff as a disciplined standing formation, though the agents and setting differ.
The immediate continuation distinguishes outward meat and blood from the taqwa intended by the sacrifice.
Defines reverence for Allah's ritual symbols as taqwa of the hearts, directly framing the budn as sha'air.
The angels' self-description as those standing in ranks reinforces the ordered sense of sawaff.
Divine subjection of the sea supplies food and calls for gratitude, paralleling the provision-and-thanks sequence.
The warning against striving against the signs adds no focused relation to sacrifice, food, or gratitude.
The sister's distant observation does not clarify the sacrificial standing or distribution in the focus.
Continual remembrance of Allah offers a general devotional parallel, without the sacrificial setting.

The list of earlier deniers does not clarify the sacrificial practice.

House-entry etiquette does not add to the focus.
The single rebuke at resurrection does not clarify the sacrificial animals.
Avoidance by the wretched does not relate to the focus.
Remembering Allah after fear offers a general worship link only.
The nearby assertion of divine strength supports the One who subjects the animals, but adds no concrete ritual detail.
The human response to favor and harm does not clarify sacrifice or feeding.
Fire as reminder and provision for travelers does not add to the focus.
Allah's disavowal of needing provision or food sharpens the focus's direction of provision from Him to people.
Avoidance of the Fire by the most pious does not clarify the focus.
It calls for eating Allah's lawful good provision and thanking Him in worship, a close broader parallel.
Calling on powerless false gods does not clarify the focus's sacrificial practice.
The tree's role as a trial does not add to the animal sacrifice reading.
Worldly desire and Hell do not clarify the focus.

The nearby call to worship and do good gives broad closing context but no sacrificial detail.
The protection of places where Allah's name is remembered supplies only a general name-of-Allah connection.
Grace rewarded with thanks offers only a general gratitude resonance.
The search for wholesome food and provision is related consumption, but not sacrifice or ritual distribution.
Divine knowledge of heaven and earth does not clarify the focus.
Permission to eat together or separately gives a limited communal-eating parallel.

Reciting remembrance has a general dhikr link but does not clarify the animal rite.

Hostile reception of recited signs does not clarify sacrifice, food, or gratitude.

The law of retaliation does not clarify the focus.
Yusuf's fulfilled vision and reunion do not add to the focus.

Counseling hypocrites does not add to the ritual provision sequence.

It directly presents livestock as divinely tamed for riding and eating, paralleling the focus's subjected animal provision.
Commands believers to eat the good provision Allah has given and thank Him, extending the focus's consumption-and-gratitude sequence.
Directly regulates the Hajj offering, including its destination and alternatives when the pilgrimage is obstructed.
Declares grazing livestock lawful while preserving the pilgrimage restriction, supplying a basic legal frame for the animals in the focus.
Its food law forbids animals dedicated to other than Allah, sharply clarifying why the focus requires naming Allah over the sacrifice.
The account of the two offerings gives sacrifice an acceptance-before-Allah horizon beyond its material act.
Requires a compensatory offering to reach the Kaaba, directly connecting livestock, sacred destination, and feeding the needy.
Names the Kaaba, sacred month, offerings, and garlanded animals together as the Sacred House's ordained order.
Rejects invented livestock categories, clarifying that ritual treatment of animals must follow Allah's ordinance rather than fabrication.
Explains Allah's food boundaries and asks why believers would not eat what His name has been mentioned over.
Explicitly forbids eating that over which Allah's name has not been mentioned, the direct negative counterpart to the focus formula.
Pairs eating from divine produce with giving its due at harvest, illuminating provision as carrying an obligation of distribution.
Identifies livestock as both carrying animals and food and commands eating from Allah's provision without following Satan.
Its enumeration of livestock pairs supplies background for the animal categories used in sacrificial provision.
Places sacrifice together with prayer, life, and death as wholly for Allah, directly grounding the focus's exclusive naming of Him.
The promise that gratitude increases divine favor supports the focus's concluding call to give thanks.
Describes livestock as created for warmth, benefits, and food, closely matching the focus's divinely provided animal benefits.
The cattle are a source of drink and nourishment, a secondary animal-provision parallel.
Its ban on what has been dedicated to other than Allah reinforces the exclusive divine orientation of the sacrifice.
The purification of the House for circumambulation, standing, bowing, and prostration establishes the sacred setting of the ensuing rites.
The command to proclaim the Hajj directly introduces the pilgrimage movement in which the focus's sacrificial rite occurs.
It closes the surah with the chosen community's religion and command to strive for Allah, providing the larger covenantal frame for its rites.
Livestock provide drink, many benefits, and food, closely paralleling the focus's animal provision before its ritual specification.
The messenger-command to eat good things and act righteously gives a broad ethical frame for consuming provision.
Allah's creation of livestock for human possession directly precedes their taming for riding and eating.
Ibrahim's commanded sacrifice of his son supplies a major Quranic sacrifice scene, marked by submission to Allah's command.
The son is ransomed with a great sacrifice, directly presenting divinely supplied sacrificial substitution.
Allah makes livestock for people to ride and eat, closely paralleling the focus's divinely subjected animal provision.
The rider's remembrance that Allah subjected the mounts and the ensuing gratitude gives a related subjection-and-thanks formula.
Feeding food to the poor, orphan, and captive provides a direct ethical parallel to the focus's command to feed others.
Its rebuke for not encouraging the feeding of the poor supplies a negative counterpart to the focus's distribution command.
Feeding during famine gives a concentrated instance of the social duty that the focus attaches to sacrificial food.
The condemnation of withholding encouragement to feed the poor contrasts directly with the focus's required feeding.
The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice is a compact, direct parallel for worship-directed sacrifice.
Its required giving to relatives, orphans, and the needy provides a broad distributional counterpart to feeding from the sacrifice.
Feeding a needy person as compensatory practice supplies a legal parallel for provision directed to those in need.
Its identification of recipients for spending gives a general social frame for the focus's command to feed others.
The instruction to spend from good earnings and what Allah brings forth supplies a broad ethic of sharing provision.
Its command to do good to relatives, neighbors, and needy people gives a general ethical horizon for sacrificial distribution.
Lawful food from the sea is a distinct food-law parallel, without the focus's naming or sacrificial setting.
It rejects arbitrary claims that the contents of certain livestock are restricted by sex, clarifying divine rather than invented food rules.
Its specified food prohibitions and ban on dedication to other than Allah provide a close legal boundary for animal consumption.
The historical livestock restrictions on the Jews are a secondary food-law contrast to the focus's permitted animal provision.
The messenger's making good things lawful and impure things forbidden offers a broad food-law frame.
Benefits from livestock skins, wool, and hair extend the Quranic presentation of animals as divine provision.
The cattle are said to provide further benefits and drink, continuing the provision sequence immediately after riding and eating.
The creation of eight livestock pairs gives background to the animal kinds available as divine provision.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is condemned, forming a clear negative counterpart to the focus's command to feed.
A recognized claim in wealth establishes a broad economic basis for provision owed to others.
It identifies the needy and deprived as holders of that claim, generally paralleling the focus's food distribution.
The admission of not feeding the poor supplies another explicit negative counterpart to the focus's feeding command.
